newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker as currency softens.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker as currency softens.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker on Friday, softening with the currency amid concern about a widely expected election call this weekend, analysts said.

"The key focus this morning is essentially the expectation of the call of the election," said Barry Davenport, senior vice-president of treasury with Bank of Monteal. He said concern about potential volatility in the dollar during a campaign has hurt the unit, which then weighed on T-bills.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.24 percent from 3.20 percent at Thursday's close.

The Canadian dollar opened easier at C$1.3954 (US$0.7166) on Friday from Thursday's close of C$1.3923 (US$0.7182) as U.S. interest rate hike fears resurfaced and investors became jittery ahead of an expected Canadian federal election call.

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien is widely expected to call an election this weekend for June 2. Davenport said the potential for dollar volatility during a campaign was highlighted in a European newspaper, which was being reflected in a weaker money market.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.66 percent from 3.63 percent on Thursday.
The one-year T-bill softened to yield 4.26 percent, from 4.19 percent at Thursday's close.
The call loan rate traded at 2.95 percent, near the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range. ((Jeffrey Hodgson (416) 941-8105, e-mail: jeffrey.hodgson@reuters.com))
